meta.title: Closing the Loop from Shop Floor to COO
meta.subtitle: A same-day operating proposal across Spacesight, Echo, Harbor Wiki, and Alivia

slides.title: Closing the Loop from Shop Floor to COO
slides.subtitle: A same-day operating proposal across 120 APAC stores and 2,000 frontline staff
slides.script: We are starting with the idea that RetailCo does not simply need more data. We believe the bigger issue is timing. If the COO learns on Monday what happened last week, the moment to intervene has already passed. The proposal we are bringing together uses Spacesight, Echo, Harbor Wiki, and Alivia as one operating loop: see the floor, hear the customer conversation, capture what works, and turn that into a decision-ready proposal. We will follow one store through a single day, before and after that loop exists.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: We should sit with this sentence because it tells us exactly where the operating model is breaking. The concern is not only that the spreadsheet is late, or that it is manual, or that it summarizes too much. The concern is that last week’s reality arrives after the team has already lived through it. A queue forms, a customer objection goes unanswered, a new hire guesses, and a manager improvises. By Monday, we can explain it, but we cannot change that day’s outcome.

slides.title: One store, one day, two operating models
bullets: Start with the Monday-lag operating model
Rebuild the day around live floor and conversation signals
Bottle the best manager's playbook into Harbor Wiki
Be explicit on scheduling as an open item
slides.script: We will follow one representative store through a trading day and compare two ways of running it. First, we look at the current Monday-lag model, where the COO receives a backward-looking spreadsheet. Then we show the same day with Spacesight and Echo feeding signals while the day is still live. We connect those signals to Harbor Wiki, so the practices of the strongest managers can be reused by new hires and weaker stores. Finally, we separate what this proposal solves from what remains open, especially staff scheduling.

slides.text: The gap is not visibility; it is the time between a store moment and a COO decision.
slides.script: We are reframing the problem from reporting to response. RetailCo already has evidence that things are different store by store: the best managers outsell the weakest by three times, onboarding takes six weeks, and rosters take coordination across many people and teams. The proposal is not to create another dashboard that explains yesterday. It is to shorten the distance between what happens on the floor and what leaders can do about it. That is why the unit of value is the same trading day, not the weekly report.

slides.title: Before: a day becomes a spreadsheet

steps.label: Open
steps.text: Managers set the floor using local habits.

steps.label: Midday
steps.text: Queues, missed approaches, and coaching moments pass unseen.

steps.label: Close
steps.text: Notes and numbers are reconstructed after the fact.

steps.label: Monday
steps.text: The COO receives last week's summary.

slides.script: In the current day, the store opens with whatever the local manager believes works. Some managers clearly have a better method, because RetailCo sees a three-times gap between the best and worst. But as the day unfolds, the moments that explain that gap are mostly invisible centrally. We do not know which customer approaches worked, which queues cost attention, or which new hire needed help. By close, everyone is reconstructing fragments. By Monday, the COO receives a spreadsheet that can describe the past, but cannot coach the day that just happened.

slides.title: After: the same day becomes an operating loop

cards.heading: Spacesight
cards.body: Sees traffic, dwell, queues, and floor execution while the day is still happening.

cards.heading: Echo
cards.body: Captures and scores what frontline staff actually say to customers.

cards.heading: Harbor Wiki
cards.body: Turns proven manager behaviors into searchable guidance for every store.

slides.script: The joined-up proposal starts by changing what the organization can sense during the day. Spacesight gives RetailCo a view of what is happening on the shop floor, not as a Monday artifact but as live operational evidence. Echo adds the customer conversation layer, so we can understand what staff actually say, not just what the sales number implies. Harbor Wiki then makes the learning reusable. When a strong manager handles a common objection or runs the floor better, that practice becomes something any store team can look up and apply.

slides.title: Why the same-day loop matters at RetailCo scale
slides.script: At 120 stores and 2,000 frontline staff, the same-day loop is important because small operating differences repeat across a very large system. The three-times manager gap tells us there is valuable know-how inside RetailCo already; it is just unevenly distributed. We do not need to invent a new theory of selling for RetailCo. We need to observe the stores that perform, hear the conversations that work, capture those patterns, and make them available quickly enough for other managers and new hires to use while customers are still in front of them.

slides.title: The same store, with the loop closed before close

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Spacesight spots floor patterns and service friction.

steps.label: Hear
steps.text: Echo identifies conversation strengths and misses.

steps.label: Teach
steps.text: Harbor Wiki serves the relevant play.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Leaders act before the day is lost.

slides.script: Now the same store runs differently. Spacesight notices the pattern on the floor, such as where customers wait or where execution breaks down. Echo adds the voice of the frontline, so we can distinguish a traffic issue from a conversation issue. Harbor Wiki connects the signal to guidance: how the best manager handles that moment, what a new hire should say, or what the shift lead should check. The COO is no longer waiting for Monday’s spreadsheet. The organization can intervene, coach, and standardize before the trading day is over.

slides.title: Every COO pain mapped honestly

rows.right: Spacesight and Echo provide same-day floor and conversation signals.
Harbor Wiki bottles the behaviors of the strongest managers.
Harbor Wiki and Echo support guided coaching from real interactions.
Open item: connect findings to workforce scheduling workflows.

slides.script: We want to be very direct about coverage. Spacesight and Echo address the COO’s first pain: knowing what actually happens on the floor before it is too late. Harbor Wiki addresses the second pain by bottling what the best managers do, and it addresses onboarding by giving new hires a consistent place to learn rather than depending entirely on whoever is working that day. Scheduling is different. None of these products is a workforce scheduling system. We should treat roster coordination as an open item, with an adjacent integration or workflow design rather than pretending it is solved here.

slides.title: Pilot output: an Alivia proposal RetailCo can act on
slides.subtitle: The pilot should produce a decision package, not just observations.
bullets: COO names a small pilot store set
Spacesight and Echo capture same-day operating evidence
Harbor Wiki seeds repeatable winning plays
Scheduling integration documented as a separate workstream
slides.script: The pilot should end with an operating decision, not a science project. That is where Alivia belongs in the proposal. Alivia takes what we learn from Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki and turns it into a client-ready rollout proposal: which signals matter, which plays should be standardized, what evidence supports expansion, and what remains out of scope. We would also use that proposal to document the scheduling workstream separately, because roster coordination is real pain for RetailCo, but it needs a workforce scheduling answer or integration path.

slides.title: Our ask: a named-store pilot
slides.subtitle: Prove the same-day loop in a small set before scaling across APAC.
bullets: Name 4 pilot stores: strong, weak, new-hire-heavy, roster-complex
Run Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki through one trading cycle
Use Alivia to produce the rollout and open-items proposal
Review evidence with the COO before broader deployment
slides.script: Our ask is to start with a small, named set of stores rather than trying to move all 120 at once. We suggest four that RetailCo names: one strong store, one weaker store, one with heavy new-hire activity, and one where roster coordination is especially painful. That gives us the right contrast without overcomplicating the pilot. We would run the same-day loop, capture what works, seed Harbor Wiki, and use Alivia to build the decision proposal. Then we review the evidence with the COO before any broader APAC rollout.

approach.angle: The real problem is not missing data, it is that nothing reaches the COO in time to act. Argue for closing the loop from floor to decision inside a single day.
approach.device: Follow one store through a single day, before and after.
approach.opener: Open on the customer's own words - put their quote on screen before anything else.
approach.close: Close by asking for a pilot in a small, named set of stores.
